title: Roadmapping AI Products Under Uncertainty
summary: Learn to build phased, hypothesis-driven roadmaps for AI products where outcomes are uncertain. This lesson shows how to balance research spikes, data acquisition, and shippable milestones using staged gates and clear success metrics.
objectives: Explain why traditional feature roadmaps fail for AI products and how uncertainty changes planning
Structure an AI roadmap into discovery, validation, and scaling phases with explicit hypotheses
Define entry and exit criteria (gates) that tie experiments to go/no-go decisions
Sequence data acquisition, model experimentation, and shipping milestones to reduce risk early
Communicate uncertainty and confidence levels to stakeholders without overcommitting on dates
Apply metrics and kill criteria to keep an AI roadmap honest and adaptive

quiz.q: Why is a traditional feature roadmap risky for AI products?
options: AI features are always cheaper to build
Feasibility is uncertain until you experiment with data and models
quiz.why: Unlike conventional software, you cannot assume an AI capability will reach its quality bar; feasibility must be validated through experimentation before you can promise outcomes.

quiz.q: What is the primary output of the Discovery/Feasibility phase?
options: A confidence signal about whether the capability is achievable
quiz.why: Discovery uses time-boxed spikes to produce evidence about feasibility—a confidence signal—not a shippable product.

quiz.q: Which sequencing principle best reduces risk early in an AI roadmap?
options: Polish the UX before testing the model
Skip baselines and go straight to complex models
Delay data work until after launch
quiz.why: De-risking means addressing the biggest uncertainty first—usually data and feasibility—before investing in downstream work like UX.

quiz.q: Why should kill criteria be defined in advance?
options: To guarantee the project never stops
To prevent sunk-cost momentum from sustaining a failing bet
quiz.why: Pre-committed kill criteria give an objective basis to stop investing, countering the sunk-cost bias that keeps doomed projects alive.

quiz.q: In one sentence, write a hypothesis-style roadmap item for an AI feature, including a measurable signal.
quiz.answer: We believe an email-classification model will correctly route support tickets for SMB customers, and we'll know we're right when auto-routing accuracy exceeds 85% with under 5% misroute escalations.
quiz.why: A good answer states the capability, the target outcome, the user segment, and a measurable signal that would confirm or falsify the bet.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of presenting unproven AI work in 'Now / Next / Later' horizons?
quiz.answer: It communicates direction and priority while honestly reflecting uncertainty, instead of committing to precise dates for work that hasn't been validated.
quiz.why: Horizons avoid false precision on uncertain work and let the roadmap update as evidence arrives, keeping stakeholder expectations realistic.

Emmanuel Ameisen, Building Machine Learning Powered Applications

body_markdown:
## Why AI Roadmaps Are Different

Traditional product roadmaps assume that if you build a feature correctly, it will work. AI products break that assumption: feasibility itself is uncertain until you experiment with data and models. You cannot promise an outcome (e.g., "95% accurate fraud detection") before you've validated it. Roadmapping under uncertainty means planning to *learn*, not just to *build*.

Key sources of uncertainty:
- **Feasibility**: Can a model actually reach the quality bar?
- **Data**: Do we have enough representative, labeled data?
- **Value**: Will users trust and adopt the AI output?
- **Cost/latency**: Is it economical and fast enough in production?

## Hypothesis-Driven Roadmapping

Frame each roadmap item as a testable hypothesis instead of a fixed deliverable:

> "We believe that [model/feature] will achieve [outcome] for [user segment]. We'll know we're right when [measurable signal]."

This reframes the roadmap from a list of promises into a sequence of bets, each with a way to be proven wrong cheaply.

## The Three-Phase Structure

1. **Discovery / Feasibility (spikes)** — Time-boxed experiments to test whether the core ML capability is achievable. Output: a confidence signal, not a product. Example: offline model evaluation on a sample dataset.
2. **Validation (thin slice)** — Ship a narrow, real version to a small audience. Test value and trust with real users (often with a human-in-the-loop fallback). Output: evidence of adoption and acceptable quality.
3. **Scaling / Hardening** — Improve reliability, reduce cost/latency, expand coverage, add monitoring and guardrails. Output: a production-grade product.

Each phase has **gates**: explicit entry and exit criteria. You only advance when evidence clears the gate; otherwise you iterate, pivot, or kill.

## Sequencing: Data and Experiments First

Reduce the biggest uncertainty earliest. Usually that means front-loading **data assessment** and **feasibility spikes** before committing UI or launch dates. A common anti-pattern is designing polished UX before knowing the model can perform.

Useful sequencing principles:
- Tackle the riskiest assumption first ("de-risking").
- Run a baseline (heuristic or simple model) before complex models.
- Treat data collection/labeling as a first-class roadmap item with its own timeline.
- Keep a manual or rules-based fallback so you can ship value while the model matures.

## Gates and Kill Criteria

Define in advance what success and failure look like. A gate might read: "Proceed to validation only if offline F1 ≥ 0.80 on the holdout set and labeling cost per item < $0.50." Equally important are **kill criteria** — the conditions under which you stop investing. Pre-committing to kill criteria prevents sunk-cost momentum.

## Communicating Uncertainty to Stakeholders

- Present the roadmap in **horizons** (Now / Next / Later) rather than precise quarterly dates for unproven work.
- Attach **confidence levels** to items (e.g., high/medium/low).
- Separate **committed** deliverables (low-uncertainty engineering) from **exploratory bets** (research spikes).
- Update the roadmap as evidence arrives; treat it as a living artifact tied to learning milestones.

## Putting It Together

A strong AI roadmap reads as a chain of de-risking decisions: identify the riskiest assumption, design the cheapest test, set a gate, and only then commit further resources. This keeps the team adaptive while still giving the business a credible path to shipping.

Unlike traditional software, AI feasibility is uncertain until you experiment. We'll cover a phased, hypothesis-driven approach that balances experimentation, data needs, and real shipping milestones.

bullets: Feasibility is unknown until you test with data and models

slides.narration: Traditional roadmaps assume that if you build a feature correctly it works. AI breaks that assumption. You don't know if a model can hit the quality bar until you experiment. There are four big uncertainties: feasibility, data availability, user value, and production cost or latency. So an AI roadmap should be designed to learn, not merely to ship a predefined feature list.

'We believe X will achieve Y for segment Z'
'We'll know when [measurable signal]'

We believe a given model or feature will achieve a specific outcome for a specific user segment, and we'll know we're right when we see a measurable signal. This turns the roadmap into a sequence of bets, each of which can be proven wrong cheaply before you over-invest.

slides.title: The Three-Phase Structure
bullets: 1. Discovery / Feasibility — time-boxed spikes
2. Validation — thin slice to real users
3. Scaling / Hardening — reliability, cost, guardrails
Each phase ends in a decision gate
slides.narration: Structure the roadmap into three phases. Discovery uses time-boxed spikes to test whether the core capability is even achievable. Validation ships a narrow real version to a small audience to test value and trust, often with a human in the loop. Scaling hardens reliability, reduces cost and latency, and adds monitoring. Between each phase sits a gate where you decide to advance, iterate, or stop.

slides.narration: Sequencing matters. Front-load the biggest uncertainty—usually data assessment and feasibility. Don't polish UX before you know the model performs. Always run a simple baseline first; sometimes a heuristic is good enough. Give data collection and labeling their own timeline, and keep a manual fallback so you can deliver value while the model matures.

slides.title: Gates and Kill Criteria

Example: proceed if F1 ≥ 0.80 and label cost < $0.50/item
Pre-commit kill criteria to avoid sunk-cost traps
Gates connect experiments to go/no-go decisions
slides.code:
GATE: Discovery -> Validation
  PASS IF offline_F1 >= 0.80
      AND label_cost_per_item < 0.50
  KILL IF F1 < 0.60 after 3 iterations
slides.narration: Define what success and failure look like before you start. A gate might say: proceed to validation only if offline F1 is at least 0.80 and labeling cost per item is under fifty cents. Equally important are kill criteria—the conditions that tell you to stop investing. Pre-committing to these prevents sunk-cost momentum from keeping a doomed bet alive.

slides.title: Communicating Uncertainty
bullets: Use Now / Next / Later horizons, not hard dates
Attach confidence levels: high / medium / low
Separate committed work from exploratory bets
Update the roadmap as evidence arrives
slides.narration: Stakeholders need honesty without panic. Present unproven work in Now, Next, and Later horizons rather than precise quarterly dates. Attach confidence levels to items. Clearly separate committed, low-uncertainty engineering from exploratory research bets. And treat the roadmap as a living artifact that updates as learning milestones produce evidence.

slides.title: Putting It Together
bullets: Identify riskiest assumption
Design the cheapest test
Set a gate with success and kill criteria
Commit further only after evidence clears the gate
slides.narration: To summarize, a strong AI roadmap is a chain of de-risking decisions. Identify the riskiest assumption, design the cheapest test to validate it, set a gate with clear success and kill criteria, and commit more resources only when evidence clears the gate. This keeps your team adaptive while still giving the business a credible path to shipping.
